fact_text:
Commonly believed: As an EEA/Norwegian national you can move to the UK and start work freely.

Actually: Since 1 Jan 2021 Norwegian nationals are treated like any other non-UK national under the points-based system. To work they normally need a Skilled Worker visa, which requires the UK employer to already hold a Home Office sponsor licence and issue a Certificate of Sponsorship (CoS). The employer's sponsor-licence application itself costs GBP 611 (small/charity) or GBP 1,682 (medium/large) and takes around 8 weeks; the role must pay at least the standard threshold of GBP 41,700/year OR the occupation 'going rate', whichever is higher.

Action required: Confirm the UK entity holds a valid sponsor licence (or start the ~8-week application) BEFORE promising a start date; validate the salary against both the GBP 41,700 floor and the occupation going rate; build CoS + visa processing time into the move timeline.

Commonly believed: Once your employee works in the UK, UK National Insurance simply applies.

Actually: The UK and Norway have a social security agreement. For a temporary posting (up to 2 years) a Norway-based employee can remain in the Norwegian social security scheme and be exempt from UK National Insurance if a certificate of coverage (PDA1) is issued by the Norwegian authority (NAV). Without the certificate, UK NICs become due and dual contributions can arise.

Action required: Decide early whether the assignment is a posting (stay in Norwegian scheme, obtain a PDA1/certificate of coverage from NAV) or a local UK hire (UK NICs apply); do not assume it defaults correctly.

Commonly believed: The NHS is free at the point of use, so no health cost for the move.

Actually: The Immigration Health Surcharge (IHS) of GBP 1,035 per year must be paid UP FRONT for the ENTIRE visa length at the point of application — e.g. GBP 3,105 for a 3-year Skilled Worker visa — before the visa is granted and before NHS access. It is separate from and on top of the visa fee.

Action required: Budget the full-duration IHS as a lump sum at application (GBP 1,035 x years) and decide up front whether employer or employee pays it.

Commonly believed: You must wait for a National Insurance number before the employee can be paid/start.

Actually: The employee can legally START WORK before the NI number arrives, provided they can prove their right to work in the UK; the NI number is applied for once in the UK and is permanent for life. Payroll can run on an emergency basis meanwhile. Delaying the start date 'until the NI number comes' is unnecessary.

Action required: Let the start date proceed on proof of right-to-work; have the employee apply for the NI number after arrival and give it to payroll when issued.

Commonly believed: UK nationals use the EU/EEA registration scheme to live and work in Norway.

Actually: After Brexit, UK nationals who move to Norway NOW are third-country nationals and canNOT use the EU/EEA registration scheme. A new mover needs a residence permit (e.g. skilled worker) — the employer must first CONFIRM the job offer (an anti-fraud step) before the application can be submitted, the job must normally be full-time (at least 80%), and a degree-level role permit is granted for up to 3 years at a time. (Only UK nationals resident in Norway before 1 Jan 2021 keep free-movement-style rights under the Separation Agreement.)

Action required: Treat a post-2021 UK hire as a third-country work-permit case: employer confirms the job offer in UDI's system first, then the employee applies for a skilled-worker residence permit before travelling to work.

Commonly believed: Working offshore in Norwegian waters means Norwegian social security applies.

Actually: A UK employer sending staff to work on the NORWEGIAN CONTINENTAL SHELF (in connection with exploration of the seabed/subsoil or exploitation of natural resources) can keep them in UK National Insurance by obtaining an HMRC certificate of coverage — the continental-shelf scenario is named explicitly in the UK-Norway arrangement. Without the certificate the worker becomes liable for Norwegian national insurance (trygdeavgift).

Action required: For any offshore/energy rotational worker, apply to HMRC for a certificate of coverage before mobilisation; keep it on file to rebut a Norwegian NI assessment.

Commonly believed: You apply for a normal Norwegian tax deduction card and are taxed under ordinary rules.

Actually: New foreign workers are AUTOMATICALLY placed into the flat-rate PAYE (Pay As You Earn) scheme in their first year / for short stays — a fixed percentage with no tax return and no deductions. It is voluntary and you must actively OPT OUT to be taxed under the general rules. You cannot use PAYE if you earn above NOK 725,050 (2026). Employees with large deductible costs may be worse off under PAYE.

Action required: Check whether the flat PAYE default is actually optimal for the employee's salary/deductions; opt out into general taxation if not, before the first tax card is issued.

Commonly believed: Everyone just gets a D-number when they first arrive to work.

Actually: A D-number becomes 'inactive' five years after it was assigned. Anyone who worked in Norway before (common in energy/maritime) and still has an old D-number must REACTIVATE it — including attending an in-person ID check with a valid passport if the D-number is five years old or more — before a new tax deduction card can be issued. This is a hidden delay that surprises returning workers.

Action required: For any employee who has worked in Norway before, check D-number status early and book the in-person ID-check appointment to reactivate it well before the first payday.

Commonly believed: As an EU/EEA citizen you must register with UDI (police) under the EEA registration scheme within 3 months.

Actually: A NORDIC citizen (Denmark) is exempt from BOTH a residence permit AND the UDI EU/EEA registration scheme under the Nordic common labour market — they may live and work in Norway freely. Skatteetaten's standard online 'Move to Norway' report also does NOT apply to movers from a Nordic country. The ambush: 'nothing to register' is false — to be paid correctly you still need a Norwegian identity number and tax deduction card, which for a stay over 6 months requires appearing IN PERSON at a Norwegian tax office to be entered in the National Population Register.

Action required: Skip UDI/EEA registration for Danish nationals, but book the in-person tax-office visit early to obtain the national identity number + tax card; do not wait for a (non-existent) UDI step.

Commonly believed: You apply for a normal Norwegian tax card and are taxed under ordinary rules.

Actually: Like all newly-arrived foreign workers, a Danish employee is AUTOMATICALLY placed into the flat-rate PAYE scheme in their first year / for short stays (fixed %, no tax return, no deductions). It is voluntary and opt-out; not usable above NOK 725,050 (2026). Not always the cheapest option.

Action required: Review whether flat PAYE or general taxation is better for the employee and opt out of PAYE if needed before the first tax card.

Commonly believed: A D-number is issued fresh on arrival.

Actually: A D-number goes 'inactive' after five years. A Danish employee who previously worked in Norway (frequent in shipping/energy) must reactivate an old D-number — with an in-person ID check if it is five years old or more — before a new tax deduction card can be issued.

Action required: Check for a pre-existing D-number and, if it is inactive, book the in-person ID-check to reactivate it before payroll onboarding.

Commonly believed: Register your address and you are set up in Denmark.

Actually: The CPR number gates almost everything — bank account, MitID, a doctor/health card, and the tax card/salary. You canNOT get a CPR number until you have a PERMANENT address you actually live at, and municipalities typically require a minimum residing period of 1-3 months for a permanent address. This creates a housing/CPR chicken-and-egg that delays payroll. (As a NORDIC citizen a Norwegian does NOT need an EU residence document first — unlike other EU nationals.)

Action required: Secure a genuine permanent Danish address first (short-term/serviced lets often do not qualify), then register for CPR at the municipality/International Citizen Service immediately on arrival.

Commonly believed: High earners can opt into a simple 27% flat expat tax.

Actually: The researcher/expat tax scheme (forskerskatteordningen) is 32.84% (27% + 8% labour-market contribution), NOT 27%, for up to 84 months. It requires a guaranteed average monthly salary of at least DKK 65,400 (2026) met FROM THE START of employment; the salary is checked continuously and a dip below the average (e.g. unpaid leave) can RETROACTIVELY disqualify you, taxing the period under ordinary rules (top marginal ~55%). No deductions are allowed, and you must not have been fully tax-liable in Denmark in the previous 10 years.

Action required: Lock the qualifying gross salary in the employment contract from day one, register the scheme via the employer, and guard against mid-year salary/leave dips that break the threshold.

Commonly believed: Open a Danish bank account when convenient.

Actually: You need a CPR number to establish a NemKonto — the single 'easy account' into which ALL Danish public payments (incl. tax refunds) are made — and you need MitID (the national eID) to access essentially every online public and banking service and your mandatory Digital Post. Sequence is strict: CPR -> MitID (via passport-chip scan in the app) -> NemKonto -> reliable salary/refund payment.

Action required: Plan the CPR -> MitID -> bank account -> NemKonto chain as the critical path; the employee cannot transact digitally in Denmark until MitID is active.

Commonly believed: As an EU citizen you have free movement, so you can just move in and register.

Actually: Unlike a Nordic citizen, a German (EU, non-Nordic) must FIRST obtain an EU residence document (registration certificate) confirming the right to reside, and only THEN can register an address and receive a CPR number. Because CPR gates the bank account, MitID, doctor and tax card, this extra front-loaded step (which Nordic movers skip) can delay the whole set-up if not started immediately.

Action required: Start the EU residence document application on/ before arrival, then register the address for CPR; do not assume EU free movement means zero paperwork.

Commonly believed: There is a simple 27% flat expat tax for incoming employees.

Actually: The forskerskatteordningen is 32.84% (27% + 8% AM contribution) for up to 84 months, conditional on a guaranteed average salary of at least DKK 65,400/month (2026) met from the start of employment and continuously; a salary/leave dip below the average retroactively disqualifies the period to ordinary tax (~55% top). No deductions; must not have been fully DK tax-liable in the prior 10 years.

Action required: Fix the qualifying salary in the contract from day one and monitor it; register the scheme via the employer to avoid a retroactive ordinary-tax reassessment.

Commonly believed: The employee opens a bank account after arriving.

Actually: A CPR number is required to establish a NemKonto (the account all Danish public payments use) and MitID (national eID) is required for nearly all online banking, public services and mandatory Digital Post. Critical path: EU residence document -> CPR -> MitID -> bank account/NemKonto.

Action required: Sequence the digital-ID chain right after CPR; salary and public refunds cannot be paid reliably until NemKonto is assigned.

Commonly believed: As an EU citizen you have free movement, so no registration is needed to settle in Germany.

Actually: You must register your home address (Anmeldung) at the local citizens' office (Bürgeramt/Meldebehörde) within 14 DAYS of moving in — a legal duty even for EU citizens who need no residence permit. Registration requires a landlord's move-in confirmation (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung); you cannot register without it. The resulting Anmeldebestätigung is the key that unlocks the tax ID, bank account and more.

Action required: Get the landlord's Wohnungsgeberbestätigung at move-in and book the Bürgeramt Anmeldung appointment immediately — slots can be scarce, and the 14-day clock is legal.

Commonly believed: You get a German tax number automatically and payroll just works.

Actually: After Anmeldung the Federal Central Tax Office (BZSt) mails the 11-digit Steuer-Identifikationsnummer (IdNo); employers use it to retrieve electronic wage-tax data (ELStAM). Until the employee gives payroll the IdNo, the employer must apply tax class VI (Steuerklasse VI) — the HIGHEST withholding — so the first paychecks are heavily over-taxed (reclaimable later). The IdNo record also stores religious affiliation, which triggers automatic church tax (Kirchensteuer, ~8-9% of income tax) if a religion is registered.

Action required: Have the employee forward the IdNo letter to payroll as soon as it arrives to move off tax class VI; brief them that early over-withholding is recovered via the annual return, and that declaring a church affiliation adds church tax.

Commonly believed: Nothing to pay unless you own/register a TV.

Actually: The Rundfunkbeitrag (public broadcasting contribution) is a MANDATORY fee of EUR 18.36 per month per dwelling — one dwelling equals one fee — owed by every household regardless of whether anyone owns a TV or radio. It is billed automatically once you register (Anmeldung); ignoring the letters leads to enforcement. Mandatory for every resident since 2013.

Action required: Budget ~EUR 18.36/month (~EUR 220/year) per household and pay/set up the Beitragsservice mandate rather than ignoring the letters.
